description: baseline: RandomForest(20 trees, depth 10) on speed_mph, grade_percent, miles
hypothesis: establishes the reference point every later experiment is measured against; no prior session exists in this tree
observation: rmse=0.013345, trip_rmse=0.003037 in 7.3s of the 600s budget
reasoning: the run uses ~1% of the time budget, so the baseline is almost certainly capacity-limited rather than data-limited — there is room for far larger models and richer features before the budget binds

description: max_depth 10 -> 20
hypothesis: the baseline forest is capacity-limited (it uses 1% of the time budget), so deeper trees should fit the heavy-tailed target better and lower both metrics
reasoning: depth 10 was already past the useful point for 3 features — the extra depth memorizes noise in the regen tail rather than signal, so the baseline is feature-limited, not depth-limited; unused time budget is not evidence of under-capacity

description: n_estimators 20 -> 100 (Pareto-better but discarded on inference cost)
hypothesis: more trees is variance reduction rather than capacity, a different knob from exp1 depth, so it should help or tie on both metrics
observation: both metrics improved but only by 0.03% (rmse 0.013345 -> 0.013341, trip_rmse 0.003037 -> 0.003036) at 5x the trees and 2x the fit time
reasoning: technically Pareto-dominant but the gain is noise-level while the inference cost is 5x per link traversal, which domain.md names as a competing objective — rejected on the cost/simplicity criterion, and it confirms exp1 that the 3-feature model is feature-limited, not model-limited

description: add one-link lookback feature prev_speed_mph (first link of journey filled with 0)
hypothesis: domain.md names acceleration as the dominant unmeasured driver of energy use and permits one backward link; the previous links speed is the only available proxy, so it should cut link error substantially
observation: rmse fell 31.3% (0.013345 -> 0.009164) while trip_rmse fell only 1.55% (0.003037 -> 0.002990); both improved so this Pareto-dominates
reasoning: the lookback is by far the biggest lever found so far, confirming acceleration was the missing signal; the lopsided split is the key insight — acceleration and braking errors largely cancel when summed along a journey, so trip totals were already near-right and the gain is almost entirely link-level precision

description: add explicit speed_delta = speed_mph - prev_speed_mph
hypothesis: a tree splits one axis at a time and cannot express a difference of two columns, so handing it the acceleration proxy explicitly should beat making it reconstruct the difference from the raw pair
observation: rmse fell 9.5% (0.009164 -> 0.008293) and trip_rmse fell 5.7% (0.002990 -> 0.002819) — both improved, and trip_rmse moved much more than it did in exp3
reasoning: representation matters as much as information for axis-aligned models: the raw pair was already present in exp3 yet the explicit difference still bought 9.5%; the larger trip_rmse move suggests the delta corrects a directional bias that accumulates along a journey rather than cancelling like exp3s gain did

description: add ke_delta_per_mile = (v^2 - v_prev^2)/(2*miles), the physics form of the acceleration term
hypothesis: specific kinetic energy change per unit distance carries the same units as the target (energy per mile), so it should map onto the target more directly than the raw speed difference from exp4
observation: rmse fell 1.0% (0.008293 -> 0.008210) and trip_rmse fell 1.06% (0.002819 -> 0.002789) — both improved, in near lockstep this time
reasoning: a real but much smaller gain than exp4, so most of the acceleration signal was already captured by the raw delta and the division by distance adds only a little; the symmetric movement of the two metrics suggests this term corrects link and trip error in the same proportion rather than targeting either tail

description: add geometry-derived sinuosity = miles / straight-line endpoint distance
hypothesis: a curvier link forces cornering and therefore braking and reacceleration at a given average speed, which the average-speed feature hides; it is also a static road attribute so it costs nothing at inference
observation: rmse fell 1.43% (0.008210 -> 0.008093) and trip_rmse fell 1.15% (0.002789 -> 0.002757); WKB decode added 23s, total run 33.8s of the 600s budget
reasoning: the geometry column carries real signal that the three scalar attributes do not, which opens the whole focus area; the gain is modest partly because links average only 3.7 vertices, so shape resolution is coarse and turn-angle style features may be limited by the same ceiling

description: add total_turn_degrees, summed absolute heading change across interior vertices (Pareto-better but discarded on simplicity)
hypothesis: sinuosity says a path is longer than the straight line but not how sharply it bends; summed turn angle should isolate the cornering that forces braking and reacceleration
observation: both metrics moved only 0.05% (rmse 0.008093 -> 0.008088, trip_rmse 0.002757 -> 0.002756) for roughly 25 lines of spherical heading math
reasoning: turn angle is almost entirely subsumed by sinuosity — with links averaging just 3.7 vertices there is little shape signal left once path-vs-straight-line ratio is known, so the coarse geometry resolution flagged in exp6 is a real ceiling on this whole feature family

description: add one-link lookback feature prev_grade_percent
hypothesis: the grade the vehicle entered the link on sets its momentum and whether it was already regenerating, completing the lookback pair alongside prev_speed_mph
observation: rmse fell 0.16% (0.008093 -> 0.008080) while trip_rmse was unchanged at 0.002757 to the harness six-decimal precision
reasoning: a genuine but small win — kept because these runs are deterministic (fixed random_state and fixed split) so 0.16% is real signal rather than noise, and the cost is 3 lines plus one precomputable feature; the flat trip_rmse says entry grade corrects individual link estimates in ways that cancel along a journey, the same cancelling dynamic seen in exp3

description: swap RandomForest for a GPU MLP (8 -> 256 -> 256 -> 1, Adam 1e-3, batch 8192, 200 epochs)
hypothesis: energy as a function of speed, grade and acceleration is smooth and continuous, which a piecewise-constant forest approximates badly; a network should fit it better and the P100 makes it affordable
observation: rmse fell 3.3% (0.008080 -> 0.007811) but trip_rmse fell 12.3% (0.002757 -> 0.002419) — by far the largest trip-level move of the session; 200 epochs finished in 110s, well inside the 400s training allowance
reasoning: the disproportionate trip gain is the real finding: a tree gives every row in a leaf the same prediction, so its per-leaf bias is systematic and accumulates when links are summed along a journey, while a smooth fit spreads error more randomly and lets it cancel — this makes smoothness, not capacity, the lever for trip_rmse; inference is now ~68k FLOPs per link versus a few hundred for the forest, so shrinking the network is worth testing as a cost reduction

description: MAX_EPOCHS 200 -> 600
hypothesis: exp9 ran all 200 epochs in 110s of a 400s allowance, so the network may not have converged and the spare budget should buy more fitting
observation: both metrics regressed: rmse +0.33% (0.007811 -> 0.007837) and trip_rmse +1.41% (0.002419 -> 0.002453); all 600 epochs completed in 262s so the time cap never bound
reasoning: 200 epochs was already past the optimum and the extra fitting overfits; trip_rmse degrades four times faster than rmse, which is the exp9 smoothness insight running in reverse — overtraining makes the fit locally bumpy, and bumpiness is exactly what accumulates when links are summed along a journey

description: cosine-anneal the learning rate to zero over the 200 epochs
hypothesis: a constant lr leaves the weights oscillating around the minimum when the loop stops; annealing to zero should settle them, and per exp10 a settled fit should pay off in trip_rmse more than in link rmse
observation: rmse fell 0.96% (0.007811 -> 0.007736) and trip_rmse fell 2.85% (0.002419 -> 0.002350) — trip moved three times further than link, as predicted
reasoning: confirms the smoothness rule from exp9/exp10 as a usable predictor rather than a post-hoc story: this was the first experiment designed from it and the metric split came out in the predicted direction and ratio; optimizer settling is cheap trip_rmse and there is likely more of it available in schedule and averaging tricks

description: MAX_EPOCHS 200 -> 400 under the cosine schedule
hypothesis: exp10s longer-training failure was diagnosed as end-of-run oscillation, which the exp11 schedule removes, so the extra epochs should now pay off instead of hurting
observation: both metrics still regressed slightly, rmse +0.19% (0.007736 -> 0.007751) and trip_rmse +0.30% (0.002350 -> 0.002357), a much smaller regression than exp10s but the same sign
reasoning: the diagnosis was wrong: 200 epochs is a genuine optimum rather than an artifact of the constant learning rate, so this network saturates on the data it has and not on fitting time — the frontier is capacity, regularization or features, and further training-length experiments are a closed direction

description: drop speed_delta — a linear layer can form the difference itself
hypothesis: speed_delta earned 9.5% for the forest only because axis-aligned splits cannot express a difference; an MLPs first linear layer forms it exactly, so the feature should now be redundant and removable at no cost
observation: both metrics improved slightly while a feature was removed: rmse -0.08% (0.007736 -> 0.007730) and trip_rmse -0.26% (0.002350 -> 0.002344)
reasoning: a simplification win — fewer inputs, cheaper inference, better numbers; the lesson generalizes past this one feature: hand-built linear combinations are crutches for axis-aligned models and become dead weight or mild noise under a network, so every remaining tree-era feature deserves the same removal test

description: drop ke_delta_per_mile, testing whether the exp13 removal lesson extends to nonlinear features
hypothesis: if hand-built features are crutches an MLP does not need, the physics term should also be removable — but it is nonlinear in three inputs, so it may be the exception
observation: both metrics regressed, rmse +0.12% (0.007730 -> 0.007739) and trip_rmse +0.38% (0.002344 -> 0.002353), the mirror image of exp13
reasoning: draws a clean boundary on the exp13 lesson: the network absorbs linear combinations of its inputs for free but does not spontaneously learn (v^2 - v_prev^2)/(2d) from speed, prev_speed and miles, so nonlinear physics terms stay valuable while linear ones become dead weight — this is the rule for choosing what to hand-engineer from here

description: add hours_per_mile = 1/speed, the auxiliary-load physics term
hypothesis: HVAC and electronics draw constant power so their per-mile cost scales with time per mile, and 1/v is a sharp nonlinearity that ReLU approximates badly near zero, so handing it over explicitly should pay under the exp14 rule
observation: a dead tie — rmse 0.007730 -> 0.007729 and trip_rmse unchanged at 0.002344 — for one extra input
reasoning: refines the exp14 rule: what matters is not nonlinearity as such but whether the term is a nonlinear *interaction across several inputs*; ke_delta_per_mile combines three columns and pays, while 1/v is a one-dimensional warp of a single input that 256 ReLU units reproduce on their own, so single-variable transforms are a closed direction

description: HIDDEN 256 -> 512
hypothesis: exp12 ruled out training time as the limit, leaving capacity as the frontier, so doubling the width should buy accuracy
observation: both metrics regressed, rmse +0.06% (0.007730 -> 0.007735) and trip_rmse +0.60% (0.002344 -> 0.002358), with trip again degrading ten times faster than link
reasoning: with time (exp12) and width both ruled out, the model is information-limited rather than model-limited, so architecture tuning is a closed direction and feature work is the only frontier left; the lopsided trip damage is the smoothness rule again — surplus capacity buys bumpiness, which trip_rmse punishes

description: HIDDEN 256 -> 128, testing whether a cheaper network holds the metrics
hypothesis: if the model is information-limited rather than capacity-limited, halving the width should cost nothing and would be a large inference-cost win under domain.mds competing-objectives clause
observation: both metrics regressed slightly and symmetrically, rmse +0.14% (0.007730 -> 0.007741) and trip_rmse +0.17% (0.002344 -> 0.002348)
reasoning: 256 is a real optimum with 512 (exp16) and 128 both worse either side of it, so width is settled and closed; worth recording that 128 costs only 0.15% for roughly a quarter of the hidden-layer FLOPs, which is the operating point to fall back to if inference cost ever binds in RouteE Compass

description: add junction_turn_degrees, the heading change from the previous links exit into this links entry
hypothesis: exp7 killed the turning *inside* a link as subsumed by sinuosity, but the turn *between* links is a different physical event — an intersection is where a driver actually brakes and reaccelerates — so it should carry signal sinuosity cannot
observation: rmse fell 4.28% (0.007730 -> 0.007399) and trip_rmse fell 1.54% (0.002344 -> 0.002308), the largest feature gain since exp5
reasoning: vindicates the exp7 post-mortem: the earlier failure was the wrong turn, not a dead geometry column, and the 3.7-vertex resolution ceiling only limits intra-link shape while junction geometry needs just two headings; it also confirms the exp16 information-limited diagnosis, since the same network that could not use more width immediately used more information

description: add one-link lookback feature prev_miles
hypothesis: a short preceding link means dense urban context with closely spaced intersections, changing how much of this link is spent accelerating away from the last one
observation: rmse fell 6.02% (0.007399 -> 0.006954) and trip_rmse fell 1.82% (0.002308 -> 0.002266) — a larger gain than junction_turn_degrees and the second biggest feature win of the session
reasoning: the urban-density story understates it; the better reading is that prev_miles tells the model how much to *trust* prev_speed_mph, because an average speed over a long previous link is a poor estimate of the speed at its end while over a short one it is a good one — the feature is a confidence weight on the lookback rather than a signal in its own right, which suggests pairing every lookback value with its own reliability context

description: add prev_hours = prev_miles / prev_speed_mph, the duration of the previous link
hypothesis: if exp19 worked because prev_miles tells the model how stale prev_speed_mph is, then duration is the sharper form of the same idea and should beat it
observation: a tie — rmse 0.006954 -> 0.006952 and trip_rmse unchanged at 0.002266 — for one more input
reasoning: the network forms this two-input ratio on its own once both parts are present, so the exp15 boundary is now firm and general: hand-engineering pays only where the term is hard to *approximate* (ke_delta_per_mile divides a squared difference by a third input), not merely where it is nonlinear; ratios of two existing inputs are a closed direction

description: signed junction turn instead of absolute
hypothesis: a left turn crosses oncoming traffic and a right turn does not, so handedness should matter; and nothing is lost by keeping the sign since a ReLU pair reconstructs the magnitude
observation: the metrics split — rmse +0.03% (0.006954 -> 0.006956) while trip_rmse fell 0.18% (0.002266 -> 0.002262) — so it fails the Pareto test despite being strictly more information
reasoning: the split is noise-level in both directions, so the honest reading is that handedness carries no usable signal; that makes sense for this data because the target is simulated over real drive-cycle traces, so any waiting at a left turn is already expressed in the traces speed profile and the sign adds nothing beyond what speed_mph and the lookback already say

description: weight the training loss by miles^2 to match the trip metric (train rows only; scoring untouched)
hypothesis: trip_rmse scores sums of rate*miles, so a links share of trip error goes as miles^2 while plain MSE treats every link alike; aligning the loss with the metric should buy trip_rmse
observation: both metrics regressed and trip_rmse got *worse* (+0.44%, 0.002266 -> 0.002276) even though it was the target of the change, with rmse +1.58%
reasoning: the miles^2 decomposition assumes link errors within a trip are independent, and they are not — per the structural insight they largely cancel, so trip error is driven by systematic bias rather than by summed variance, and reweighting shrinks the effective sample without touching the bias; this also rules out predicting energy_gge instead of the rate without testing it, since MSE on rate*miles is exactly this miles^2-weighted loss

description: add prev_sinuosity, the shape of the preceding link
hypothesis: a curvy preceding link means the vehicle was already cornering on entry, which bears on how much of prev_speed_mph actually carried through — the exp19 reliability idea applied to shape
reasoning: the lookback family keeps paying and is now complete — speed, grade, miles and sinuosity are all shifted, and the junction turn consumes the previous links exit heading, so with a strict one-link limit there is nothing left to shift; further feature gains have to come from a new source rather than from more lookback

description: ReLU -> SiLU for a smoother fit
hypothesis: a ReLU network is piecewise linear so its fit has kinks, and if local bumpiness is what trip_rmse punishes then a smooth activation should buy trip_rmse more than link rmse
observation: both metrics regressed, rmse +0.36% (0.006859 -> 0.006884) and trip_rmse +0.18% (0.002252 -> 0.002256) — and trip moved *less* than link, the opposite of the predicted signature
reasoning: an important correction to the smoothness rule: what mattered in exp9 and exp11 was systematic bias over a *region* of feature space, which is what accumulates when a journeys links are summed, not the analytic smoothness of the fit at a point; ReLU kinks sit far below the scale at which that bias operates, so the rule should be read as about regional bias and not applied to activation choice

description: add a third hidden layer
hypothesis: width is settled either side of 256 but depth was never tested, and depth changes the inductive bias rather than just the parameter count
reasoning: depth joins width and training length as closed, so the architecture is fully settled at 2x256 ReLU and every remaining knob on the model itself has now been tested and rejected; with guesswork exhausted the next move should be diagnostic — find where the residual error actually concentrates rather than proposing more features blind

description: average an ensemble of 3 independently fit MLPs (Pareto-better but discarded on inference cost)
hypothesis: the exp25 diagnostic found no systematic bias left in feature space, so the remaining error is fitting variance plus irreducible noise, and averaging independent fits attacks the variance part
observation: both metrics improved — rmse -0.54% (0.006859 -> 0.006822) and trip_rmse -0.75% (0.002252 -> 0.002235) — for 3x the inference cost and a 363s run
reasoning: discarded on the same inference-cost grounds as exp2, since energy is evaluated at every link traversal in a shortest-path search and tripling that for 0.6% is a poor trade; the scientifically important part is how *small* the gain was — if fitting variance were a real share of the remaining error, averaging three fits would have bought far more than 0.6%, so this confirms the model is close to the information ceiling available under the one-link-lookback inference constraints

description: BATCH_SIZE 8192 -> 4096
hypothesis: 8192 is a large batch for 1.3M rows and smaller batches carry more gradient noise, which acts as implicit regularization and often generalizes better
observation: the metrics split — rmse +0.39% (0.006859 -> 0.006886) against trip_rmse -0.13% (0.002252 -> 0.002249) — and the run took 249s against 148s
reasoning: fails the Pareto test, and the direction of the split is the informative part: extra gradient noise slightly helped the trip metric while hurting link accuracy, which fits the pattern that the two metrics respond to different things rather than to overall fit quality

description: BATCH_SIZE 8192 -> 16384
hypothesis: exp27 showed smaller batches hurt link rmse, so the gradient-noise argument runs the other way and a larger batch giving a cleaner gradient should help it
observation: the metrics split in the same shape as exp27 — rmse +0.17% (0.006859 -> 0.006871) against trip_rmse -0.18% (0.002252 -> 0.002248) — despite moving the batch size in the opposite direction
reasoning: both directions hurt link rmse, so 8192 is a genuine optimum and batch size is closed; that both directions nudged trip_rmse down by a similar sliver says those trip movements are at the resolution floor of the metric rather than a real response, and is a caution against reading sub-0.2% trip changes as signal

description: LEARNING_RATE 1e-3 -> 2e-3
hypothesis: batch size is settled but the learning rate it pairs with was never tuned, and a larger step under the cosine schedule may reach a better basin
observation: the metrics split in the same shape yet again — rmse +0.26% (0.006859 -> 0.006877) against trip_rmse -0.09% (0.002252 -> 0.002250)
reasoning: three optimizer knobs in four experiments (batch down, batch up, lr up) all produced the same signature of slightly worse link rmse and a sliver better trip_rmse, so the current settings sit at a local optimum and optimizer tuning is closed as a direction; combined with architecture being closed at exp25, everything except information is now exhausted

description: add vertices_per_mile, how finely the road geometry is drawn
hypothesis: sinuosity is a length ratio while vertex density is a different statistic that stands in for road class, and the exp25 diagnostic put 46% of the remaining error below 23 mph where urban-versus-highway character matters most
reasoning: modest but a genuine keep, and it matters more as evidence than as a gain: after five straight architecture and optimizer failures, the first thing to work again was new information, confirming the information-limited diagnosis holds even this late; it also shows the geometry column was not exhausted by sinuosity, since a second statistic over the same vertices still had something to add

description: drop prev_grade_percent, a tree-era feature originally kept on a 0.16% gain
hypothesis: prev_grade_percent was added under the RandomForest for a marginal 0.16% and the model family has changed twice since, so it may now be dead weight like speed_delta was in exp13
observation: both metrics regressed, rmse +0.29% (0.006837 -> 0.006857) and trip_rmse +0.22% (0.002248 -> 0.002253) — it is worth roughly twice as much now as when it was added
reasoning: a feature that was marginal under the forest became clearly worthwhile under the network, the opposite trajectory to speed_delta; entry grade only pays once the model can combine it smoothly with the rest of the lookback, so marginal keeps should be re-tested rather than pruned after a family change — value moves in both directions

description: add corner_energy_per_mile = v^2 * turn / miles, the junction braking term
hypothesis: the speed a driver sheds into a turn and rebuilds out of it scales with v^2 and turn sharpness spread over the link, giving the same three-input nonlinear shape as ke_delta_per_mile — the one feature form that has kept paying
reasoning: the three-input nonlinear *shape* is not itself what made ke_delta_per_mile valuable — that term works because it is the dominant physics of the target, not because of its functional form; copying the form onto a secondary effect gains nothing, so the exp14 rule is necessary but not sufficient and physical importance has to come first

description: signed-log compress ke_delta_per_mile to fix its conditioning
hypothesis: the raw term spans several orders of magnitude so standardizing it sets the scale from rare outliers and squashes typical values against zero; a signed log keeps ordering and sign while giving the network a resolvable input
reasoning: the conditioning argument was wrong because it ignored what the tail means: a large speed change over a very short link genuinely is a large energy rate, so the raw term is close to linear in the target and compressing it destroys exactly that relationship; with a heavy-tailed target, matching the targets own scale behaviour beats making the input well-conditioned

description: add a linear skip connection from inputs straight to the output
hypothesis: much of the physics is close to linear in the right variables — grade is potential energy per mile, ke_delta_per_mile is acceleration energy per mile — so a skip lets a linear model carry that exactly while the hidden layers fit only the nonlinear remainder
reasoning: the hidden layers were already representing the linear part accurately, so factoring it out changed nothing worth having; taken with exp24, exp25 and exp34 the architecture is now closed against inductive-bias changes as well as against size changes

description: add link_bend_degrees, the links own net heading change from entry to exit
hypothesis: a link can be long and gently curving with low sinuosity yet still swing the vehicle through a large net heading change, so net bend is distinct from both sinuosity and the exp7 summed interior turns
observation: an exact tie to six decimals on both metrics for one extra input
reasoning: with links averaging 3.7 vertices the net bend is nearly determined by sinuosity, so this is the exp7 result reached by a second route and it closes intra-link shape for good; the geometry column now has exactly two useful statistics, sinuosity and vertices_per_mile, plus the junction turn that needs the lookback

description: AdamW with weight decay 1e-4
hypothesis: regularization is the one model-side knob never tested, and decoupled weight decay is its cleanest form; per the structural rule a better-regularized fit should show up mainly in trip_rmse
observation: rmse tied exactly at 0.006837 while trip_rmse fell 0.27% (0.002248 -> 0.002242)
reasoning: kept because it is Pareto-dominant at literally zero cost — a one-word optimizer swap, no extra inference work, no new feature; the metric split is the predicted signature again, with regularization buying trip_rmse and leaving link rmse alone, and it is the first thing to work since exp30 which makes weight decay worth pushing further

description: WEIGHT_DECAY 1e-4 -> 1e-3
hypothesis: weight decay at 1e-4 was the first thing to help since exp30, so more of it may buy more of the same trip_rmse gain
observation: the metrics split, rmse +0.04% (0.006837 -> 0.006840) against trip_rmse -0.09% (0.002242 -> 0.002240), and the trip movement is below the resolution floor established in exp28
reasoning: 1e-4 is the right magnitude and an order of magnitude more starts trading link accuracy away; the trip gain here is smaller than the one from the first 1e-4 despite ten times the decay, so the mechanism has saturated rather than scaling

description: add dropout 0.1 between the hidden layers
hypothesis: weight decay helped in exp36, so a second and stronger form of regularization should help too and should again show up mainly in trip_rmse
observation: the sharpest divergence since exp9 — rmse improved 0.31% (0.006837 -> 0.006816) while trip_rmse regressed 3.26% (0.002242 -> 0.002315)
reasoning: dropout trains an average over subnetworks but predicts with the full scaled network, and that mismatch is a *systematic* offset rather than random per-link noise, which is precisely what accumulates when a journeys links are summed; regularization is therefore not one direction — weight decay shrinks weights without biasing the prediction and helps trip, dropout biases it and is the worst thing tried all session for trip_rmse

description: drop sinuosity, testing whether vertices_per_mile subsumes it
hypothesis: sinuosity and vertices_per_mile are both computed from the same vertices and both stand in for road character, so the newer one may have made the older redundant
observation: both metrics regressed sharply, rmse +2.37% (0.006837 -> 0.006999) and trip_rmse +0.89% (0.002242 -> 0.002262) — the largest regression from removing a single feature all session
reasoning: the two geometry features measure genuinely different things and are complements rather than substitutes — sinuosity is how bent the path is, vertex density is how finely it is drawn, and a straight highway drawn with many points is not a winding street; sinuosity is the more valuable of the two by roughly seven times

description: add LayerNorm after each hidden layer
hypothesis: normalization should ease optimization, and unlike dropout or BatchNorm a LayerNorm is a deterministic per-sample transform so it carries none of the train-versus-predict mismatch that wrecked trip_rmse in exp38
observation: the metrics split, rmse +0.07% (0.006837 -> 0.006842) against trip_rmse -0.04% (0.002242 -> 0.002241), both below the resolution floor
reasoning: the mismatch reasoning held — LayerNorm did not damage trip_rmse the way dropout did — but there was no optimization problem to fix in a two-layer network on standardized inputs, so it bought nothing either; architecture and normalization are now comprehensively closed

description: fill first-link prev_speed_mph with the links own speed instead of 0
hypothesis: a 0 fill tells the model the whole first link was one long acceleration from rest, whereas the vehicle is at its average speed for most of the link, so an own-speed fill implying zero acceleration should describe the average better
observation: both metrics regressed slightly, rmse +0.01% (0.006837 -> 0.006838) and trip_rmse +0.22% (0.002242 -> 0.002247)
reasoning: the original from-rest fill is right and the reasoning behind the change was wrong: a trip start genuinely is an acceleration from rest, that is real physics the model can use, and flattening it to zero acceleration throws the information away; only 0.9% of rows are trip starts yet the choice still moved trip_rmse measurably, because every trip has exactly one

description: MAX_EPOCHS 200 -> 300 now that weight decay regularizes
hypothesis: exp12 found 200 epochs optimal without regularization, and weight decay should push the overfitting point later, so the two settings ought to interact
reasoning: they do not interact — 200 epochs is optimal with and without weight decay, so the limit is not overfitting capacity being reached but the cosine schedule being tuned to complete over exactly the epochs it is given; that makes epochs and schedule one setting rather than two, and it is settled
